summary:
Second pass, now reading each report against the memory it saw going in and the memory it produced after (the two collapsible panels per card). The memory loop is the big new lens, and it reframes the headline problem.

THE CENTRAL INSIGHT: the coach's own analysis never becomes memory. The memory writer rebuilds the profile from the runner's stated facts (check-in notes + chat) plus the coach's own report digests. So when a report writes 'was the 7x400 the planned interval session?' as an open question, that open question flows into the digest, into memory's 'lately', and back into the next report, which asks it again. It is a self-reinforcing loop that only an explicit runner statement ('yes, that was the session, and 169 held') can break. The coach analysed the 8x300 (Jun 30) and the 7x400 (Jul 7) in rich, correct detail, but because that analysis is the coach's conclusion rather than the runner's stated fact, it never closes the loop. You can watch this directly: the 'lately' line survives across the Jul 5, Jul 6, and both Jul 9 memory panels essentially unchanged.

THE MEMORY SUBSTRATE OTHERWISE WORKS. The diffs show it graduating real facts correctly: the right-shin soreness moves from the July check-ins into 'limits_and_constraints', the cutback-week and rest-day-intentional character appears, goals stay stable. So the fix is narrow: give the coach a way to write a settled conclusion back as a fact (or have the prompt stop re-asking a question the run data already answers), not rebuild the memory system.

STILL THE TOP PROBLEMS (unchanged by the memory lens):
1. BLIND TO PER-RUN DISTANCES (critical). The Jul 7 Evening Ride thread: the coach cannot see individual run distances, only aggregates, and asks the runner for a long-run distance that is in our own DB. Highest-value fix.
2. ROLLING-7D vs CALENDAR-WEEK + WANDERING NUMBERS (critical/concern). The coach uses the wrong week frame, then its weekly target slides (25 to 22 km) as the runner feeds it corrections.
3. STALE INTERVAL LOOP (concern), now explained by the memory mechanism above.
4. MEDICATION HR-DISCOUNT MAYBE OVER-APPLIED (concern). Every afternoon RPE/HR gap resolves to 'HR inflated, trust RPE', even on an 8.9 km run at 159 avg / 178 max.
5. REPORT-PER-ACTIVITY SAMEYNESS (minor). ~4 activities/day, each a long near-identical easy-session report.

Protect: the interval rep-by-rep analysis (Jun 30, Jul 7) is the product at its best. Highlights below mark the specific spans; hover a highlight for the why. Process: `make coach-review` to re-pull, edit this notes file, re-render with --from-json --notes.

0a36232e-8086-4c15-8d5b-71e943113298.note: THE key thread (18 messages), and the clearest single argument for the #1 fix. The coach cannot see per-run distances, asks the runner for a number in our own DB, and its weekly recommendation wanders as the runner supplies corrections. Memory panel note: nothing here graduates a durable fix, because the gap is data the coach never receives, not memory.

highlights.quote: just the aggregate weekly numbers. Do you remember how long it was?
highlights.why: Asks the runner for a distance that is sitting in our own database. The per-run distance blindness in one sentence.

highlights.quote: not individual distances broken out per run
highlights.why: Confirms the coach only receives aggregates and effort labels, not the per-run distances a volume plan needs.

highlights.quote: Can’t you see from the data?
highlights.why: The runner's trust visibly slipping. This is the friction the data gap creates.

highlights.quote: The 10% rule would put your weekly cap closer to
highlights.why: The weekly target slid from 25 km to 22 km only after the runner supplied last week's actual total. The math wandered because the coach was guessing.

dadb8d9b-9e3d-4f4c-ab71-cf176aa4e951.note: The self-reinforcing loop in miniature. The interval work (300s Jun 30, 400s Jul 7) has already happened and been analysed, yet the coach re-asks. Runner corrects the day and the coach admits it had the date pegged wrong.

highlights.quote: The data just labels it by date so I had it pegged wrong.
highlights.why: Loose day-of-week grounding; the coach reasons about Monday/Tuesday but maps it to the wrong date.

fe9c2165-57cd-4ed2-8069-ee5e2bcfe64c.note: Open the memory panel: 'lately' still carries 'Open: 7x400m session completed July 7, confirm whether this was the planned 1k rep interval session'. The report faithfully re-asks it. That open question has now survived unchanged across four consecutive memory rebuilds because no runner statement ever closed it and the coach's own analysis cannot.

highlights.why: Stale: the coach wrote a full rep-by-rep analysis of this exact 7x400 session two days earlier. The memory loop keeps it open.

highlights.quote: 0.4% drift over the whole run, against your own baseline of around 4%
highlights.why: Clean, grounded calibration read against the runner's own norm.

e5452023-84bc-4c63-a79f-d25f47ecbc5f.note: The pattern-scan blind spot: the coach says no structured rep work is visible, but the June 30 8x300 interval session had already happened and been analysed under v13. Its own recent_training scan does not recognise an interval session it coached.

highlights.quote: nothing pops as structured rep work from the pattern I can see
highlights.why: The June 30 8x300 interval session already happened and was analysed; the coach's own scan misses it.

c3c8948a-209a-4172-ba6b-18955a181faa.note: The medication-discount question in its strongest form: an 8.9 km hilly run, avg HR 159, max 178, real Z3/Z4 time, resolved entirely to 'HR inflated, trust RPE 3'. The load_spike flag DID fire and was handled well, so the safety net worked; the concern is that the RPE/HR gap always resolves one way.

highlights.quote: the HR is doing its own thing while the actual effort felt genuinely easy
highlights.why: 8.9 km at 159 avg / 178 max with real Z3-Z4 time, called genuinely easy on RPE 3 alone. The gap never resolves toward 'maybe RPE is under-reported'.

highlights.quote: let the next day or two be genuinely easy
highlights.why: Load_spike flag caught the step-up off the cutback week and the coach gave the right, specific recovery call.

db2288ed-a094-4a4c-aeae-8ec655872ba3.note: A full, thoughtful report for a 30-min easy indoor ride that was the runner's 4th session of the day. Representative of the volume problem: ~4 activities/day, each getting a long near-identical easy-session write-up. Candidate for a lighter touch on cross-training.

highlights.why: When the report itself says there is nothing to fix, a full multi-paragraph write-up may be more than the session warrants.

5f43937f-b5ee-4ed6-86a8-3ec817e593ef.note: Exemplar, protect this. Rep-by-rep read of the 8x300 with the HR-recovery collapse, and it flagged rep 3's 111s anomaly which the runner then confirmed in chat was a deliberate watch pause. This is the product working exactly as intended.

highlights.quote: Fifteen to twenty beats lower, for faster work.
highlights.why: Sharp read: the second half ran faster at lower HR, the signal that the session found its gear once rests lengthened.

highlights.quote: The mystery of rep 3 (111 seconds vs ~65-70 for the others) solved
highlights.why: Closed the loop cleanly on the anomaly the runner explained, then carried it into next week's plan.

ecb90eee-23c0-4adc-8faa-f11501b000b5.note: Second exemplar (7x400, lean_v1). Note the tension with the memory loop: this superb analysis exists in full, yet the memory thread still treats the interval session as unconfirmed. The analysis is right there; it just never becomes a fact memory can cite.

highlights.quote: you found your real ceiling by briefly running past it
highlights.why: Excellent framing of the pacing arc: opened too fast, paid for it mid-set, self-corrected.

highlights.quote: Six beats in 89 seconds means you were going into those reps still elevated
highlights.why: Concrete, mechanism-level read of why the middle reps sagged.
